title: Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
objectives: Define node, root, leaf, height and depth for binary trees and count nodes in a perfect tree
Trace preorder, inorder, postorder and level-order traversals and state what each preserves
State the BST invariant and trace search and insert on concrete values
Explain how sorted insertion degenerates a BST to a linked list and why balanced trees exist
Relate tree height to operation cost: O(h) for search, insert and delete
motivation: Hash tables give you O(1) expected lookup but nothing else - no ordering, no neighbors, no ranges. The moment a desk asks 'all strikes between 90 and 110', 'the best bid' or 'the successor of this order', you need a structure that keeps data ordered at search speed: the binary search tree. It is also the gateway to every hierarchical structure in this track - heaps, tries, segment trees - so the vocabulary and the traversal mechanics here are used for the rest of the curriculum.

blocks.md: A **binary tree** is a hierarchy where each node holds a value and up to two children, called left and right. The top node is the **root**; nodes with no children are **leaves**; the **depth** of a node is its distance from the root and the **height** of the tree is the depth of the deepest node. A **perfect** binary tree of height $h$ (all levels full) holds $2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... per level, so 15 nodes fill exactly 4 levels. The crucial counting fact: a tree of height $h$ can hold at most $2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes, so $n$ nodes always allow a tree of height $\lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil - 1$ - **logarithmic height is achievable**, and everything else in this lesson is about securing it.

A traversal visits every node exactly once; the four canonical orders differ in *when* the node itself is visited relative to its subtrees. **Preorder** (node, left, right) copies a tree or serialises its structure. **Inorder** (left, node, right) is the star for BSTs: it visits values in ascending sorted order. **Postorder** (left, right, node) evaluates children before parents - perfect for freeing memory or computing subtree aggregates. **Level-order** sweeps the tree depth by depth with a queue (the FIFO structure from the previous lesson), which is how you find shallowest-first answers.

blocks.caption: All four traversals on one tree. Inorder on a BST reads the values sorted - the invariant's signature.
Search for 6 walks a single path: 8 -> 3 -> 6, comparing at each node and choosing a subtree - the cost is the path length, not the tree size.

blocks.text: The BST invariant and its payoffs

blocks.md: A **binary search tree** adds one rule: for every node, **all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are larger** (duplicates go to one fixed side, by convention the right). The rule turns search into a guided walk: compare against the root, discard half the tree, recurse. Insertion is the same walk ending in an empty slot; deletion has three cases (leaf: unlink; one child: splice; two children: swap in the inorder **successor** - the smallest key of the right subtree - then delete it there). Every operation costs $O(h)$: search, insert, delete, plus $O(h)$ for min, max, predecessor and successor. That $h$ is the whole game.

blocks.caption: Insert and search are the same descent - the only question is where it stops.

blocks.title: Worked example: inserting 5, 2, 9, 1, 7, 12
items: 2: $2 < 5$ -> left child of 5. 9: $9 \ge 5$ -> right child of 5.
1: $1 < 5$, $1 < 2$ -> left child of 2. 7: $7 \ge 5$, $7 < 9$ -> left child of 9.
Shape: 5 has children 2 and 9; 2 has 1; 9 has 7 and 12. Height 2 (3 levels) for 6 nodes - near-perfect, because the input arrived scattered.
Inorder walk: 1, 2, 5, 7, 9, 12 - sorted, as the invariant promises. Search for 7 touches 3 nodes ($5 \to 9 \to 7$).

blocks.md: Insert the same six values **in sorted order** - 1, 2, 5, 7, 9, 12 - and each new key is larger than everything present, so it always goes right: the tree collapses into a right-going chain, a linked list with extra memory. Height $n$ means $O(n)$ search - all the tree's advantages gone, and inserts still pay pointer overhead. The fix is **self-balancing**: AVL and red-black trees rotate locally on insert/delete to keep height $O(\log n)$ guaranteed (C++ `std::map` is a red-black tree; Python has none built-in - use `sortedcontainers` or a skip list). The payoff is making the worst case equal the expected case: $O(\log n)$ search with ordering intact - exactly what hash tables cannot offer. A balanced BST of 1,000,000 keys has height about 20; an unbalanced one can need 1,000,000 comparisons.

blocks.title: Why order-aware lookup matters on a desk
blocks.md: An order book needs the best bid *and* where the next level sits; a curve needs all strikes in a range; a risk engine needs the successor of a threshold. Hash tables answer point queries only. Balanced BSTs (or their array-coded cousins, the heaps and Fenwick trees of the next lesson) answer all three in $O(\log n)$ - which is why `std::map` on price keys, not `unordered_map`, backs many level-management implementations.

guidedExercise.prompt: Build a BST by inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 in order. (a) Draw the resulting tree. (b) Give the preorder, inorder and postorder sequences. (c) How many comparisons does search(60) take? (d) The tree is perfect - state its height and node count relationship.
hints: Each insert descends from the root and lands in the first empty slot that satisfies the invariant.
Traversal orders differ only in where the node is recorded relative to its two recursive calls.
A perfect tree of height h has 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) Root 50; 30 and 70 as its children; 20, 40 under 30; 60, 80 under 70 - one node per slot, all levels full. (b) Preorder: 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80. Inorder: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 - sorted. Postorder: 20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50 (subtrees fully before their parents). (c) search(60): compare 50 (go right), 70 (go left), 60 (found) - 3 comparisons, i.e. the depth of the node plus 1. (d) Height 2 with $2^{2+1} - 1 = 7$ nodes: perfectly balanced, so every operation costs at most 3 comparisons - the logarithmic ideal this lesson is aiming at.

independentExercise.prompt: Insert 10, 5, 15, 2, 7, 12, 17, then 1, into an initially empty BST (duplicates go right; here all values are distinct). (a) Draw the tree after the first seven inserts. (b) Draw it again after inserting 1 - where does it land and what is the new height in levels? (c) Give the inorder sequence after all eight inserts. (d) How many nodes does search(12) touch? (e) Explain in one sentence why inserting 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1 in order would be a disaster.
hints: Insert each value by descending from the root; only the path to its slot changes.
1 is smaller than everything except nothing - follow left pointers until an empty slot.
Inorder on any BST is sorted regardless of shape.
independentExercise.solution: (a) 10 root; children 5 and 15; 5 has 2 and 7; 15 has 12 and 17 - a perfect tree of 3 levels (height 2). (b) 1: $1 < 10 \to$ left, $1 < 5 \to$ left, $1 < 2 \to$ left -> left child of 2. The deepest path now has 4 nodes, so the tree has 4 levels (height 3) with 8 nodes - still near-minimal. (c) Inorder: 1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 17 - sorted, shape irrelevant. (d) search(12) touches 10 (go right), 15 (go left), 12 (found) - 3 nodes. (e) Inserting ascending keys sends every element right, producing a chain of height $n-1$: search and insert degrade to $O(n)$ and the structure is a linked list - the degenerate case that motivates AVL/red-black balancing.

commonMistakes: Mixing up traversal orders: preorder records the node before its subtrees, inorder between them, postorder after them.
Assuming inorder yields sorted output for any binary tree - only when the BST invariant holds.
Forgetting that BST operations cost O(h), not O(log n) - the log holds only for balanced trees.
Deleting a two-child node by removing it directly - you must promote the inorder successor (or predecessor) to preserve the invariant.
Confusing height (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path) with node count or level count.
realWorldApplication: Databases and file systems keep ordered indexes in balanced trees (B-trees are their disk-sized cousins), C++ std::map is a red-black tree, and every autocomplete, range-query or 'next item after X' feature over sorted data leans on tree ordering.
quantFinanceApplication: Order-book level management maps price keys to queues of resting orders in a balanced BST (or skip list): best bid/ask is the tree's min/max, the touch's successor is the next level, and a cancel is an O(log n) delete - operations a hash table simply cannot answer in order.
summary: Binary trees are hierarchies of nodes with up to two children; height h permits at most 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes, so log-height trees can hold any n.
Preorder, inorder, postorder differ in when the node is recorded; inorder on a BST reads keys in sorted order, level-order uses a queue.
The BST invariant (left subtree smaller, right subtree larger) makes search, insert, delete, min, max and successor all O(h).
Sorted insertion degenerates a BST into a linked list of height n; AVL/red-black rotations keep height O(log n), making the worst case logarithmic.

quiz.prompt: Which traversal visits the keys of a BST in ascending order?
quiz.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree (all smaller), then the node, then the right subtree (all larger) - recursively, that is exactly ascending order. The BST invariant, not the traversal, does the work.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print? (insert goes left if strictly smaller, else right)
quiz.explanation: Inserts build the BST 8 (3 (1, 6), 10 (r: 14)); the inorder walk - left, node, right - reads 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 14, which is exactly the input sorted. That is the BST invariant showing itself through traversal.

quiz.prompt: A perfect binary tree has 15 nodes. How many levels does it have?
quiz.explanation: A perfect tree of L levels holds 2^L - 1 nodes: 1, 3, 7, 15 - so 15 nodes means L = 4 levels (1 + 2 + 4 + 8). Equivalently height h = 3 edges with 2^(h+1) - 1 = 15.

quiz.prompt: Inserting the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order into an unbalanced BST produces what shape, and what is search(5)'s cost?
options: A balanced tree, O(log n) search
A right-leaning chain of height 4, O(n) search
A left-leaning chain of height 4, O(n) search
quiz.explanation: Each key is the largest so far, so every insert walks right to the end: the result is a chain (a linked list wearing a tree costume) of height n-1 = 4, and finding 5 requires comparing all 5 nodes. This degenerate case is what AVL/red-black trees prevent with rotations.

quiz.prompt: Select every true statement about the BST invariant (left subtree smaller, right subtree larger).
options: It guarantees the minimum is found by following left pointers from the root.
It guarantees inorder traversal is sorted.
It guarantees the tree is balanced.
It makes search a root-to-leaf path that discards one subtree at each node.
quiz.explanation: The invariant fixes ordering properties - min at the leftmost node, sorted inorder, halving searches - but says nothing about shape: balance needs rotations (AVL/red-black) or lucky input order, so option 3 is false.

quiz.prompt: A perfectly balanced BST holds 1,023 keys. What is the maximum number of node comparisons a search can take?
quiz.explanation: 2^10 - 1 = 1023 keys fill exactly 10 levels, so the deepest search touches 10 nodes - one comparison per level. Unbalanced, the same 1,023 keys could require up to 1,023 comparisons.

flashcards.back: For every node: all keys in the left subtree are smaller, all keys in the right subtree are larger - recursively, at every node, not just the root's children.
Inorder: sorted output (BST). Preorder: copy/serialise structure. Postorder: children before parents (deallocate, aggregate). Level-order: shallowest first via a queue.

flashcards.front: Node capacity of a perfect binary tree of height h
flashcards.back: 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes (levels hold 1, 2, 4, ...). Conversely n nodes always fit in height about log2(n) - logarithmic height is achievable.

flashcards.front: Why do AVL and red-black trees exist?
flashcards.back: Plain BSTs degenerate to linked lists under sorted insertion (O(n) operations); rotations on insert/delete keep height O(log n) guaranteed, so worst-case search/insert/delete stay logarithmic.
